def: Bohr's model explains the stability and spectrum of the hydrogen atom by assuming that electrons revolve around the nucleus only in certain fixed orbits with quantised angular momentum.
points: Postulate 1: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular orbits; the centripetal force is provided by electrostatic attraction between electron and nucleus.
Postulate 2: Only those orbits are allowed for which angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/2pi, i.e. L = n h / (2 pi), where n = 1, 2, 3...
Postulate 3: While in these allowed (stationary) orbits, the electron does not radiate energy, so the atom is stable.
Postulate 4: The atom emits or absorbs a photon only when an electron jumps from one allowed orbit to another; the photon energy equals the energy difference between the orbits.
This model successfully explained the discrete line spectrum of hydrogen.
formula: L = m v r = n h / (2 pi);  h v = Ei - Ef

diagram.draw: Draw a small nucleus at the centre. Draw three concentric circular orbits around it labelled n=1, n=2, n=3. Show an electron on orbit n=3 with an arrow jumping inward to orbit n=1, and label the emitted photon arrow 'hv'.

example: For hydrogen in n=1 orbit, angular momentum L = h/(2 pi) = 1.05 x 10^-34 kg m^2/s.
tip: List all four postulates in order — this is a standard 'state Bohr's postulates' question worth full marks for correct sequencing.

t: Energy levels and spectral series of hydrogen
def: In the Bohr model, the hydrogen atom has discrete (quantised) energy levels, and transitions of the electron between these levels produce distinct spectral lines grouped into series.
points: Energy of the nth orbit is En = -13.6 / n^2 eV (negative sign shows the electron is bound).
n = 1 is the ground state (lowest, most negative energy); higher n means higher (less negative) energy.
When an electron jumps from a higher level ni to a lower level nf, a photon of energy Ei - Ef is emitted.
Lyman series: transitions ending at n=1 (ultraviolet region).
Balmer series: transitions ending at n=2 (visible region).
Paschen, Brackett and Pfund series: transitions ending at n=3, 4, 5 respectively (infrared region).

diagram.draw: Draw horizontal lines stacked with increasing spacing getting closer together, labelled n=1 (bottom) up to n=infinity (top). Draw downward arrows between levels showing transitions to n=1 labelled 'Lyman series' and transitions to n=2 labelled 'Balmer series'.

example: Energy of n=2 level: E2 = -13.6/4 = -3.4 eV. Transition from n=3 to n=2 releases energy = (-1.51) - (-3.4) = 1.89 eV, a Balmer line.
tip: Remember the series names in order (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen) with their final energy level — a common one-mark question.

t: Nuclear size, density and mass defect
def: The atomic nucleus is an extremely small, dense core of an atom, and mass defect is the small reduction in mass when nucleons combine to form a nucleus, converted into binding energy.
points: Nuclear radius R depends on mass number A as R = R0 A^(1/3), where R0 = 1.2 x 10^-15 m (1.2 fm).
Nuclear volume is proportional to A (since R^3 is proportional to A), so nuclear density is nearly the same for all nuclei.
Nuclear density is enormous, about 2.3 x 10^17 kg/m^3, independent of the element.
Mass defect (delta m) is the difference between the sum of masses of free protons and neutrons and the actual mass of the nucleus.
delta m = [Z mp + (A-Z) mn] - M(nucleus), where Z is atomic number, A is mass number.
This 'missing' mass is released as binding energy when the nucleus forms, as per E = delta m c^2.
formula: R = R0 A^(1/3);  delta m = [Z mp + (A-Z) mn] - M;  E = delta m c^2

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Z protons and N neutrons separate"] --> B["Sum of individual masses"]
  B --> C["Nucleus forms, mass decreases by delta m"]
  C --> D["Binding energy released E = delta m c squared"]

example: For helium-4 (Z=2, A=4): sum of nucleon masses = 4.0330 u, actual nucleus mass = 4.0015 u, so delta m = 0.0315 u, giving binding energy about 29.3 MeV.
tip: Always convert mass defect from atomic mass units to energy using 1 u = 931.5 MeV in numericals.

def: Binding energy per nucleon is the binding energy of a nucleus divided by its number of nucleons; it measures how tightly nucleons are bound and indicates nuclear stability.
points: Binding energy per nucleon = total binding energy / mass number A.
A graph of binding energy per nucleon versus mass number A rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks near A = 56 (iron region), then slowly decreases for heavy nuclei.
Nuclei near the peak (iron, nickel) are the most stable.
Fusion of light nuclei (like hydrogen into helium) releases energy because binding energy per nucleon increases.
Fission of heavy nuclei (like uranium) also releases energy for the same reason — moving towards the stable middle region.
This curve explains why both fusion and fission can release nuclear energy.
formula: Binding energy per nucleon = (delta m c^2) / A

diagram.draw: Draw a graph with mass number A on the x-axis and binding energy per nucleon (MeV) on the y-axis. Show the curve rising steeply from A=1, peaking around A=56 (label 'Fe, most stable'), then gradually decreasing towards A=240. Mark arrows showing 'fusion' region on the left and 'fission' region on the right, both pointing towards the peak.

example: Iron-56 has binding energy per nucleon about 8.8 MeV, near the maximum, which is why iron nuclei are extremely stable.
tip: Draw the BE/A vs A graph with the peak at A=56 clearly marked — this diagram is asked very frequently.

t: Radioactive decay law and half life
def: The radioactive decay law states that the number of radioactive nuclei decreasing per unit time is proportional to the number of nuclei present at that time, leading to exponential decay.
points: Rate of decay: -dN/dt = lambda N, where lambda is the decay constant (characteristic of the isotope).
Solving this gives N = N0 e^(-lambda t), where N0 is the initial number of nuclei.
Half-life (T1/2) is the time in which half the radioactive nuclei decay; T1/2 = 0.693 / lambda.
Activity (A = lambda N) also decreases exponentially in the same way as N.
After n half-lives, the remaining fraction is (1/2)^n of the original amount.
SI unit of activity is becquerel (Bq); older unit is curie (Ci).

diagram.draw: Draw a graph with time t on the x-axis and number of undecayed nuclei N on the y-axis. Draw a smooth curve starting at N0 and decreasing exponentially, never touching the x-axis. Mark the time T1/2 on the x-axis where N falls to N0/2, and 2T1/2 where it falls to N0/4.

example: A sample with N0 = 1000 nuclei and half-life 10 days: after 30 days (3 half-lives), N = 1000 x (1/2)^3 = 125 nuclei remaining.
tip: For numericals, use N = N0 (1/2)^(t/T) when t is a whole multiple of half-life; otherwise use the exponential form with lambda.

def: Radioactive nuclei become stable by spontaneously emitting alpha particles, beta particles, or gamma rays, each changing the nucleus in a different way.
points: Alpha decay: nucleus emits an alpha particle (helium nucleus, 2 protons + 2 neutrons); mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number by 2.
Beta-minus decay: a neutron converts into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino; atomic number increases by 1, mass number unchanged.
Beta-plus decay: a proton converts into a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino; atomic number decreases by 1, mass number unchanged.
Gamma decay: an excited nucleus (after alpha or beta decay) emits high-energy gamma photons to reach its ground state; both A and Z remain unchanged.
Alpha particles have the least penetration power but most ionising power; gamma rays have the most penetration but least ionising power.
These decays follow conservation of mass number, charge, and energy in each nuclear reaction.
formula: Alpha: ZX^A -> (Z-2)Y^(A-4) + alpha;  Beta-minus: n -> p + e- + antineutrino

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Unstable nucleus"] --> B["Alpha decay: emits He nucleus"]
  A --> C["Beta decay: emits electron or positron"]
  A --> D["Gamma decay: emits high energy photon"]
  B --> E["Daughter nucleus, A down by 4, Z down by 2"]
  C --> F["Daughter nucleus, Z changes by 1, A same"]
  D --> G["Same nucleus, lower energy state"]

example: Uranium-238 undergoes alpha decay: U-238 (Z=92) -> Th-234 (Z=90) + alpha particle (He-4).
tip: Practise writing balanced nuclear equations showing conservation of both mass number and atomic number on both sides.
